title: What JavaScript is (compared to C# and TypeScript)
hook: JavaScript is the language browsers and Node.js actually run. TypeScript only checks types before they disappear. C# compiles to Intermediate Language (IL) for the Common Language Runtime (CLR). Knowing which host runs your code prevents costly mix-ups in interviews and on the job.

blocks.text: JavaScript is a dynamically typed language standardized as ECMAScript. A JavaScript engine — such as V8 in Chrome and Node.js, SpiderMonkey in Firefox, or JavaScriptCore in Safari — parses your source, compiles it, and runs it. There is no separate compile step you ship to production in the typical web workflow: you deliver JavaScript (or a bundle) and the engine executes it. TypeScript is a superset that adds static types on top of JavaScript; after `tsc` or a bundler runs, only JavaScript remains. C# is a statically typed language whose types survive compilation into IL metadata enforced by the CLR — a completely different runtime host.

entries.plainDefinition: The official specification that defines JavaScript syntax and built-in behavior. New features ship as ECMAScript yearly editions (ES2015, ES2020, and so on).
entries.example: Arrow functions and `const`/`let` were standardized in ECMAScript 2015.

entries.plainDefinition: The program inside a browser or Node.js that parses, compiles, and executes JavaScript. V8 is the most widely discussed engine.
entries.example: Node.js bundles V8; Chrome uses V8 directly.

entries.plainDefinition: The environment that provides APIs beyond the language itself — the browser DOM, Node.js file system, or the CLR for C#.
entries.example: `document` exists in the browser host, not in bare ECMAScript.

blocks.text: If you treat JavaScript like "C# without types" or TypeScript like "C# that compiles to something else," you will misunderstand errors, performance, and deployment. A Redis client in C# holds a real typed object at run time. A TypeScript interface describes shape only until JavaScript runs. When you ship an Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) consumer as a Node.js Lambda, the host is V8 — not the CLR. Same JSON event, different process, different type system, different garbage collector, different concurrency model.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: JavaScript is what the engine executes. TypeScript type-checks then erases. C# compiles to IL for the CLR with real types. Three different layers — do not collapse them.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: You write JavaScript (or TypeScript that becomes JavaScript)
items.body: Variables have no fixed static type at the language level. The engine discovers types as values flow through your program.

items.title: The engine parses and compiles
items.body: Modern engines use Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation: bytecode first, then optimized machine code for hot paths — unlike C# where Roslyn emits IL before the CLR ever loads.

items.title: The host provides APIs and scheduling
items.body: Browser or Node.js adds timers, network, file I/O. JavaScript's single-threaded event loop coordinates async work — the CLR uses threads and a thread pool instead.

diagram.title: JavaScript vs C# / TypeScript hosts
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph jsts [JS/TS path]
    TS[TypeScript optional] --> JS[JavaScript source]
    JS --> V8[V8 or other engine]
    V8 --> CPU1[Machine code]
  end
  subgraph csharp [C# path]
    CS[C# source] --> Roslyn[Roslyn compiler]
    Roslyn --> IL[IL + metadata]
    IL --> CLR[CLR host]
    CLR --> CPU2[Machine code]
  end

snippet.label: Dynamic typing at run time
snippet.explanation: JavaScript does not reject the reassignment. The engine tracks the current value's type at run time. C# would fail at compile time because `int` and `string` are incompatible in the type system.

snippet.label: TypeScript erases at compile time
snippet.explanation: TypeScript interfaces exist only for the checker. C# interfaces and classes are real types in the assembly the CLR loads. At run time, both JavaScript and erased TypeScript see a plain object.

snippet.label: Same JSON, different runtime types
snippet.explanation: Both handlers receive the same SQS JSON, but only C# preserves nominal types through deserialization into assembly-defined classes. JavaScript only has structural duck typing.

snippet.label: Host APIs are not part of ECMAScript
snippet.explanation: ECMAScript defines `console` loosely and core types. `document`, `fs`, and `fetch` come from the host. C# Base Class Library (BCL) types are part of the .NET platform similarly, but through assemblies on the CLR.

blocks.title: JavaScript vs C# / TypeScript at a glance
rows: Threads + thread pool + async/await on Task

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Saying JavaScript is "untyped" — it has dynamic types at run time (`typeof`, `instanceof`). Assuming `tsc` is analogous to `dotnet build` — tsc erases types; Roslyn emits typed IL. Calling a Node.js Lambda handler "the same as .NET" because both receive JSON — the deserializer still produces plain objects, not CLR types. Expecting TypeScript interfaces to exist at run time for `instanceof` checks.

interviewTakeaways: JavaScript is dynamically typed at run time; TypeScript adds compile-time checks that erase before execution; C# keeps real types in IL metadata enforced by the CLR.
Three layers to name for JS: ECMAScript language, engine (V8), host (browser or Node.js) — not the CLR.
In production polyglot systems, the contract is JSON Schema or OpenAPI — never assume TS interfaces match C# DTOs without codegen.
60s: JavaScript runs on V8 in Node or the browser. Types are discovered at run time. TypeScript erases to JS. C# compiles to IL with CLR enforcement. Same SQS JSON, different hosts and type systems.
Follow-up: how does `JSON.parse` differ from `System.Text.Json.Deserialize` at the type level?
commonPitfalls: Saying JavaScript has no types — it has dynamic run-time types; it lacks static compile-time enforcement like C#.
Assuming tsc output is like a .NET assembly — tsc erases; Roslyn emits typed IL.
Strong answer: 'JS engine executes source with dynamic types. TS erases. C# CLR keeps metadata. Polyglot needs schema contract.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# runs on the CLR with threads and a generational garbage collector. JavaScript runs on an engine with a single-threaded event loop. Same microservice payload, different process model.
TypeScript types exist only at compile time. C# types remain as metadata the CLR uses. JavaScript never had those types to begin with.
